1:
Keil (grammatical-historical) sets the section in the book’s plan: with the wall finished, Nehemiah secures the city, then repopulates it, then orders civil life by the law, and last puts the Levites’ service in order at the dedication. Hanging the doors completes the fortification; the gatekeepers, singers and Levites are then given the charge, which he restricts to the watching of walls and gates, since it was anciently the doorkeepers’ office to keep watch over the house of God. Henry (puritan-evangelical) reads the appointment the other way, of their temple work, neglected and now revived: dead walls without living watchmen are a poor defence, and God’s worship is itself a city’s defence, his ministers being the watchmen of Isaiah 62:6. He allows the narrower reading too, that they were made ready against the dedication, and turns it into a principle: what is devoted to God is what is likely to do us good.

Two men are put over the city, and the witnesses divide over which of them the commendation belongs to. Henry takes them as a pair — the one Nehemiah’s own brother, who had brought him the news of the desolation at Nehemiah 1:2; the other formerly ruler of the palace, promoted because a man faithful in less is trusted with more — and refers the commendation to Hananiah. Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) refers it to Hanani, and works it into a list of qualifications for office: a faithful man believes rightly in God’s government and is devoted to his people, and one who fears God above many will govern by the laws, guard religion, and neither oppress nor take bribes. Henry draws another lesson from the phrase: among those who truly fear God some fear him greatly, and are owed the double honour of Psalms 15:4. Clarke and Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) agree on why the appointment was made at all — Nehemiah was about to return to the Persian court.

The order about the gates draws three readings of one phrase. Gill (reformed) takes until the sun be hot as the heat of the day, near noon, or at least long enough after sunrise for the light to be full, so that an ambush could be seen and the townsmen be up and armed. Wesley puts it at clear and broad day, when the people would be ready for an assault. Clarke reads it much earlier, as simply not before sunrise, the gates being shut again at sunset, and supports it from a custom still kept in eastern cities of his own day, where a traveller arriving after dark must lodge in the plain until morning. Keil renders the whole order together: the doors are shut and locked while the watch is still at its post, and the citizens keep guard, some at watch-posts and some before their own houses. Clarke and Keil agree that each man was answerable for the wall opposite his own door, and Keil notes that the verb used here for closing the doors occurs nowhere else in Hebrew.

The last verse states the problem the rest of the chapter answers. Gill measures it: the wall followed its old foundation and enclosed as much ground as ever, and he sets an ancient estimate of fifty furlongs beside Josephus’ thirty-three. Keil is careful about what the complaint says. The city was broad on both sides, measured from the centre either way, and the words about houses do not mean there were none, since the place had been inhabited again for ninety years, but that building had not kept pace with the circuit of the walls. That is the gap Nehemiah is about to address, and Keil takes the next verse to say where the resolution came from, God having put it into his heart.
5:
Nehemiah credits the plan to God, and every witness stops on it. Gill (reformed) calls it his habit: whatever he thought conducive to the good of Jerusalem, he ascribed to God. Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) puts the habit into a sequence: if he purposed good it was because God put it into his heart, if he did good it was because the good hand of his God was upon him, if he expected good it was because he had prayed God to remember him. Henry (puritan-evangelical) generalises it: every good motion in the mind, prudent or pious, comes from above, and what looks like human prudence must be credited to providence, since the God who teaches the husbandman his discretion at Isaiah 28:26 teaches the statesman his. Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) says the same in two sentences that follow Henry almost word for word. Keil (grammatical-historical) is the one who asks what the resolution actually was: to assemble the nobles and rulers so that the people could be reckoned by genealogy, and so to get a basis for the repopulation the previous verse showed to be necessary.

Henry explains why a census answers a defence problem. The safety of a city depends less on the height of its walls than on the number and courage of the people inside them; an account of the families would show which had once been settled in Jerusalem and drifted into the country, and might be brought back, and which others could be drawn in by religion or trade to rebuild and live there. He turns it into a maxim of national policy: the balance between capital and country should be kept even, the metropolis neither so large that it drains the country nor so weak that it cannot protect it.

What Nehemiah found was a register, and the witnesses disagree about whose. Keil takes those who came up at the first to mean the return under Cyrus with Zerubbabel and Jeshua rather than the later company with Ezra, and states that the list which follows is identical with the one in Ezra 2. Clarke reads it as older still, a register of people who came long before Zerubbabel and therefore one that could not answer to the state of the nation in Nehemiah’s day, since some families had died out and others arrived; on that view Nehemiah revised it only in parts, which is what produces the differences. He also declines to annotate the list, since it is almost the same as the earlier chapter.

The differences are the real question, and two answers are offered. Gill proposes a mechanism: the earlier list was drawn up in Babylon, when those intending to travel gave in their names, and this one after arrival; so some who registered changed their minds, some died on the road, which lowers certain figures, and others who had not registered followed after, which raises others. Henry canvasses the alternatives and rejects the obvious one first: he will not accept that the earlier list gives the families at their coming and this one as they stood forty years later, since so many households could not have remained almost unaltered for so long. He prefers either the mistakes of copyists, which happen easily with numbers, or a difference between the copies the two compilers used; and he allows Gill’s explanation as a third possibility, one list taken at the setting out and the other at the arrival. He notes that the totals agree throughout except for the singing men and women, two hundred in the one place and two hundred and forty-five here. Behind the arithmetic he sees a purpose: the register kept the families distinct until the Messiah came, and its repetition shows the notice God takes of his people by name.
19: Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) is the only witness to stop on this line, and he stops on a single digit. The text as it stands numbers the children of Bigvai at two thousand and sixty-seven; some manuscripts read two thousand and sixty-six, which is the figure the parallel register carries at Ezra 2:14. He records the variant without adjudicating it, which is his practice through this list wherever the copies part. Henry (puritan-evangelical), reviewing the register as a whole rather than line by line, describes exactly this pattern — most of the numbers identical between the two chapters and a few differing by one or two — and treats such small divergences as the ordinary work of copyists, numbers being the easiest thing in a manuscript to miscopy.
33: Twice in two lines the register says the other, and Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) takes up both. On the men of the other Nebo he observes that the qualifying word is absent from the parallel register at Ezra 2:29 and missing from many manuscripts here, so that its presence in this copy is itself uncertain; and he identifies the place with Nob, or Nobah, in the territory of Benjamin. On the other Elam, in the following line, the word is doing plain work: it distinguishes this family from the Elam already entered earlier in the same list. The two notes pull in different directions. Where the second use of the word has an obvious function, the first may be no part of the text at all, which is why Clarke handles them separately rather than treating the repetition as a single feature of the register.
68:
The tail of the register raises textual questions before it raises devotional ones, and Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) is almost the only witness who takes them up. He reports that the verse numbering the horses is missing from some fifty manuscripts in one collation and twenty-nine in another, from a sixteenth-century printed Hebrew text, from the Roman edition of the Septuagint, and from the Syriac and the Arabic — though he is careful to add that the Arabic proves little here, since it omits the whole list and keeps only the first five verses of the chapter. The verse does stand in the parallel register at Ezra 2:66. A verse later he records a different kind of intrusion: Jerome added to the Vulgate a line marking where the document ends and the historian resumes, to the effect that thus far run the words written in the register and what follows belongs to Nehemiah’s own history. Clarke notes that the sentence appears in neither the Hebrew nor any ancient version, and is absent from the great Polyglots, though it stands in the first printed Vulgate. He adds one more variant, that where the text gives the silver in pounds a Greek copy reads three hundred minae rather than two.

On the offerings themselves the witnesses divide over a small phrase with a large consequence. Gill (reformed) reads the giving straightforwardly: the chief of the fathers gave toward the work of building city and temple, and what went to the treasure was the fund from which the temple’s expenses and its service were met; he values the people’s twenty thousand drachms of gold at as many pounds and somewhat more. Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) identifies the Tirshatha as Nehemiah and takes him to be the donor. Clarke points out that a Septuagint copy reads it the other way, that the sum was given to the Tirshatha for the treasury, which reverses the direction of the whole transaction.

Whether this is even the same collection as the one recorded in the earlier register is a further question, and the two who address it disagree. Wesley says plainly that it is another collection, which is why the figures do not match Ezra 2:68. Henry (puritan-evangelical) feels the difficulty more sharply — there the governor is not mentioned at all, here he opens the subscription, and the single sum named there exceeds everything listed here put together — yet he concludes it probably was the same contribution reported from a different copy of the lists, since the closing verse of the chapter matches the close of the earlier one. He then sets the whole dispute in its place: faith and hope do not rest on the niceties of names and numbers, and what is given to the work of God is not forgotten, down to a cup of cold water.

Clarke closes on what the register was for. The examination was undertaken precisely so that the families could be traced, and through the families the towns and villages that belonged to them under the ancient division of the land; and he dates the operation, since the wall was finished in the sixth month at Nehemiah 6:15 and the last verse of this chapter finds the people settled in their own cities in the seventh. About a month, then, from the survey to the settlement. His verdict on the method is the point of the chapter: the register decided everything, so that there was no room for complaint and nobody could accuse the governor of partiality. Gill notes only that the closing verse repeats the earlier register word for word.
